subject: Mathematics
title: Isha's Architecture: Polygons, Shapes, and Symmetry
hook: Isha designs buildings and discovers that shapes have hidden patterns—sides, angles, and perfect reflections.

slides.title: Exploring Some Geometric Themes
slides.storyContext: Isha designs a new school building in Bangalore. Each room has different shapes—rectangles, pentagons, hexagons. Mr. Patel teaches her the properties of each and the hidden symmetries.

slides.title: The Design Challenge
slides.storyContext: Isha sketches: square classrooms, triangular roofs, hexagonal lunch hall. Rohan asks: "Why hexagons?" Mr. Patel explains: "Hexagons are strong, efficient, and have beautiful symmetry. Let me teach you about polygons."

slides.title: Polygons: Sides, Vertices, and Angles

points.label: Definition
points.text: A polygon is a closed plane figure made of straight line segments. The sides don't cross. Vertices are the corners where sides meet.

points.label: Naming
points.text: Triangles (3 sides), quadrilaterals (4), pentagons (5), hexagons (6), heptagons (7), octagons (8), nonagons (9), decagons (10).

example.problem: How many vertices does a hexagon have?
example.solution: A hexagon has 6 sides and 6 vertices (one at each corner).

slides.inSimpleWords: A polygon is a closed shape made of straight sides. The number of sides = number of vertices.

slides.title: Sum of Interior Angles

points.label: Formula
points.text: For any polygon with n sides, the sum of interior angles = (n - 2) × 180°.

example.problem: What is the sum of interior angles in a pentagon?
example.solution: Pentagon has 5 sides. Sum = (5 - 2) × 180° = 3 × 180° = 540°.

slides.inSimpleWords: To find the sum of all angles inside a polygon: count sides (n), subtract 2, multiply by 180°.

slides.title: Regular Polygons: All Sides and Angles Equal

points.label: Definition
points.text: A regular polygon has all sides of equal length and all angles of equal measure. Examples: equilateral triangle, square, regular hexagon.

points.label: Each angle in a regular polygon
points.text: Each interior angle = [(n - 2) × 180°] / n.

example.problem: What is each interior angle in a regular octagon?

slides.inSimpleWords: A regular polygon looks the same no matter how you rotate it. All sides are equal, all angles are equal.

slides.title: Line Symmetry: Mirror Images

points.label: Definition
points.text: A shape has line symmetry if it can be folded along a line so that both halves match perfectly. That line is called a line of symmetry.

points.label: Examples
points.text: Square: 4 lines of symmetry. Rectangle: 2. Circle: infinite. Equilateral triangle: 3. Isosceles triangle: 1.

example.problem: How many lines of symmetry does a regular hexagon have?
example.solution: A regular hexagon has 6 lines of symmetry: 3 through opposite vertices and 3 through midpoints of opposite sides.

slides.inSimpleWords: Line symmetry means you can fold the shape along a line and both halves look identical.

slides.title: Rotational Symmetry: Spinning Into Place

points.label: Definition
points.text: A shape has rotational symmetry if it looks the same when rotated less than 360° around a central point. The order of rotational symmetry is how many times it matches itself in one full rotation.

points.label: Examples
points.text: Square: order 4 (matches at 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°). Equilateral triangle: order 3. Regular hexagon: order 6.

example.problem: A shape matches itself when rotated 60°. What is its order of rotational symmetry?
example.solution: 360° / 60° = 6. The shape has rotational symmetry of order 6 (like a regular hexagon).

slides.inSimpleWords: Rotational symmetry means the shape looks the same when you spin it around. The more it matches itself, the higher the order.

slides.title: Properties of Common Quadrilaterals

points.label: Square
points.text: 4 equal sides, 4 right angles (90°), diagonals equal and perpendicular. 4 lines of symmetry, rotational symmetry of order 4.

points.label: Rectangle
points.text: Opposite sides equal, 4 right angles, diagonals equal but not perpendicular. 2 lines of symmetry, rotational symmetry of order 2.

points.label: Rhombus
points.text: 4 equal sides, opposite angles equal, diagonals perpendicular. 2 lines of symmetry, rotational symmetry of order 2.

points.label: Parallelogram
points.text: Opposite sides equal and parallel, opposite angles equal. No line symmetry, but rotational symmetry of order 2.

example.problem: A shape is a rectangle. How many lines of symmetry does it have?
example.solution: A rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry (one through the midpoints of opposite long sides, one through midpoints of opposite short sides).

slides.inSimpleWords: Different quadrilaterals have different symmetries. Squares have the most; general parallelograms have the least.

image.alt: Properties of Common Quadrilaterals — Exploring Some Geometric Themes

slides.title: Isha's Hexagon Lunch Hall
slides.storyContext: Isha designs a regular hexagon-shaped lunch hall. Mr. Patel asks: find the sum of interior angles and the number of symmetries.

example.problem: A regular hexagon: find sum of interior angles and number of lines of symmetry.
example.solution: Sum = (6 - 2) × 180° = 720°. Each angle = 720° / 6 = 120°. Lines of symmetry = 6 (3 through vertices, 3 through edge midpoints).

slides.inSimpleWords: Regular hexagons are strong and symmetric—perfect for buildings.

slides.title: Your Turn: The Tile Pattern
slides.storyContext: Isha tiles a floor with regular octagons and squares. How many lines of symmetry does a regular octagon have?

example.problem: Find the sum of interior angles in a regular octagon and its line symmetry.
example.solution: Sum = (8 - 2) × 180° = 1080°. Each angle = 135°. Lines of symmetry = 8 (4 through opposite vertices, 4 through edge midpoints).

slides.inSimpleWords: Regular octagons also tile well and have high symmetry.

slides.title: Triangles: The Foundation of Every Building
slides.storyContext: Rohan points to the roof trusses. 'Why are these triangular, Uncle?' Mr. Patel smiles. 'Triangles are the strongest shapes—they can't be pushed out of shape like other polygons. They're everywhere in architecture.'

slides.title: Types of Triangles by Sides

points.label: Equilateral Triangle
points.text: All 3 sides are equal in length. All 3 angles are equal (each 60°). Has 3 lines of symmetry.

points.label: Isosceles Triangle
points.text: Two sides are equal in length. Two angles are equal (the base angles). Has 1 line of symmetry.

points.label: Scalene Triangle
points.text: All 3 sides have different lengths. All 3 angles are different. Has no line symmetry.

example.problem: In an isosceles triangle, two sides are 5 cm each and the third is 6 cm. If one of the equal angles is 65°, find the third angle.
example.solution: In an isosceles triangle, the two base angles (opposite the equal sides) are equal. Both base angles = 65°. Third angle = 180° - 65° - 65° = 50°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Triangles are named by their sides: all equal (equilateral), two equal (isosceles), or all different (scalene).

slides.title: Types of Triangles by Angles

points.label: Acute Triangle
points.text: All three angles are less than 90°. Example: angles of 60°, 60°, 60°.

points.label: Right Triangle
points.text: One angle is exactly 90°. The side opposite the right angle is the hypotenuse (longest side).

points.label: Obtuse Triangle
points.text: One angle is greater than 90°. Only one obtuse angle is possible in a triangle.

example.problem: A triangle has angles 90°, 45°, and 45°. What type is it?
example.solution: Since one angle is 90°, it's a right triangle. Since two angles are equal (45° each), it's also isosceles. It's an isosceles right triangle.

slides.inSimpleWords: Triangles are also sorted by their angles: all sharp (acute), one corner-like (right), or one very wide (obtuse).

slides.title: Isha's Floor Design Discovery
slides.storyContext: Isha notices that triangular floor tiles fit perfectly together, leaving no gaps. 'Look!' she exclaims to Mr. Patel. 'These right triangles lock together like a puzzle!' He nods. 'That's because their angles add up perfectly. Let me show you the patterns.'

slides.title: Congruent and Similar Shapes

points.label: Congruent Shapes
points.text: Two shapes are congruent if they have the same size and shape—you can place one exactly on top of the other.

points.label: Similar Shapes
points.text: Two shapes are similar if they have the same shape but different sizes. Corresponding angles are equal; corresponding sides are proportional.

points.label: Notation
points.text: Congruent: △ABC ≅ △DEF. Similar: △ABC ~ △DEF.

example.problem: Triangle ABC has sides 3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm. Triangle DEF has sides 6 cm, 8 cm, 10 cm. Are they congruent or similar?
example.solution: They are similar, not congruent. Each side of DEF is exactly 2 times the corresponding side of ABC (6=2×3, 8=2×4, 10=2×5). The shapes match but sizes differ.

slides.inSimpleWords: Congruent shapes are identical twins; similar shapes are the same shape but different sizes, like a photo and an enlarged poster.

slides.title: Understanding Diagonals

points.label: Definition
points.text: A diagonal is a line segment connecting two non-adjacent vertices of a polygon.

points.label: Number of diagonals
points.text: For a polygon with n sides, the number of diagonals = n(n-3)/2.

points.label: Examples
points.text: Square (n=4): 4(4-3)/2 = 2 diagonals. Hexagon (n=6): 6(6-3)/2 = 9 diagonals.

example.problem: How many diagonals does a pentagon have?
example.solution: Pentagon has 5 sides. Number of diagonals = 5(5-3)/2 = 5(2)/2 = 5 diagonals.

slides.inSimpleWords: A diagonal connects two corners of a shape that aren't next to each other. Different shapes have different numbers of diagonals.

slides.title: Perimeter and Area Basics

points.label: Perimeter
points.text: The total distance around a shape. For any polygon, add up all the side lengths.

points.label: Area
points.text: The space inside a shape, measured in square units (cm², m², etc.).

points.label: Triangle area
points.text: Area = (1/2) × base × height.

points.label: Rectangle area
points.text: Area = length × width.

example.problem: A triangle has a base of 10 cm and a height of 8 cm. Find its perimeter if the sides are 10 cm, 10 cm, and 12 cm.

slides.inSimpleWords: Perimeter is how far you walk around the edge; area is how much space the shape covers inside.

slides.title: Symmetry Saves the Day
slides.storyContext: During the construction, Isha notices an error in the octagonal room design. 'Wait!' she tells the workers. 'If we use the lines of symmetry as guides, we can check if both halves are identical!' The workers are amazed at how she spots the mistake.

slides.title: Point Symmetry (Rotational Center)

points.label: Definition
points.text: A shape has point symmetry if it looks identical when rotated 180° around a central point.

points.label: Center of symmetry
points.text: The point around which the shape is rotated. If a point on the shape is at distance d from the center, its symmetric point is also at distance d on the opposite side.

points.label: Examples
points.text: Square: has point symmetry. Rectangle: has point symmetry. Equilateral triangle: does not have point symmetry.

example.problem: Does a regular hexagon have point symmetry? Explain.
example.solution: Yes. When rotated 180° around its center, each vertex maps to the opposite vertex, and the hexagon looks identical.

slides.inSimpleWords: Point symmetry means if you spin the shape halfway (180°) around its center, it looks exactly the same.

slides.title: Tessellations: Shapes That Tile

points.label: Definition
points.text: A tessellation (or tiling) is a pattern of shapes that fit together perfectly with no gaps or overlaps.

points.label: Regular tessellations
points.text: Using only one type of regular polygon. Only three work: equilateral triangles, squares, and regular hexagons.

points.label: Why it works
points.text: The interior angles must divide evenly into 360° (the angles around a point).

example.problem: Can you make a tessellation with regular pentagons? Explain using interior angles.
example.solution: No. A regular pentagon has each interior angle = 108°. 360° ÷ 108° = 3.33..., which is not a whole number. So pentagons won't fit perfectly around a point.

slides.inSimpleWords: Some shapes like squares and hexagons can tile perfectly together with no gaps. Others like pentagons cannot.

slides.title: Isha's Complete Building Plan
slides.storyContext: Isha presents her final design: a square foundation with an octagonal garden and triangular roof trusses, all symmetric and perfectly tessellated.

example.problem: A building has: (1) A square base with side 20 m, (2) An octagonal garden inside with each interior angle = 135°, (3) Triangular supports. Find: (i) Area of square base, (ii) Sum of angles in octagon, (iii) Each angle in octagon.
example.solution: (i) Area of square = 20 × 20 = 400 m². (ii) Sum of angles in octagon = (8-2) × 180° = 1080°. (iii) Each angle = 1080° / 8 = 135°.

slides.inSimpleWords: By combining different polygons and understanding their properties, Isha creates a building that's both beautiful and structurally sound.

slides.title: Three-Dimensional Shapes from Polygons
slides.storyContext: Isha learns that when you stack or combine polygons, you create 3D shapes. 'A cube is made of 6 squares! A pyramid is made of a square base and triangles!' she exclaims.

points.label: Polyhedra
points.text: 3D shapes made of flat faces (polygons). Each face is a polygon; edges connect vertices.

points.label: Common polyhedra
points.text: Cube (6 squares), rectangular prism (6 rectangles), triangular pyramid (1 triangle base, 3 triangle sides), square pyramid (1 square, 4 triangles).

points.label: Euler's formula
points.text: For any polyhedron: Vertices − Edges + Faces = 2. (V − E + F = 2)

example.problem: A cube has 8 vertices and 12 edges. How many faces does it have?
example.solution: Using Euler's formula: 8 − 12 + F = 2, so F = 6. A cube has 6 faces (all squares).

slides.inSimpleWords: 3D shapes are built from 2D polygons as faces. Stacking triangles, squares, and other shapes creates pyramids, prisms, and more.

slides.title: Angles in a Circle: A Special Polygon
slides.storyContext: Mr. Patel draws a circle and says: 'A circle is like a polygon with infinite sides, each infinitely small. It has special angle properties.'

points.label: Central angle
points.text: An angle at the center of a circle. A full rotation = 360°.

points.label: Inscribed angle
points.text: An angle formed by two chords from a point on the circle. It equals half the central angle subtending the same arc.

points.label: Arc measure
points.text: Arcs of a circle are measured in degrees (0° to 360°).

example.problem: A central angle in a circle is 80°. What is the inscribed angle subtending the same arc?
example.solution: The inscribed angle = (1/2) × central angle = (1/2) × 80° = 40°.

slides.inSimpleWords: A circle has 360° total. Angles at the center and angles on the rim have a special relationship.

slides.title: Design Your Own Symmetric Building
slides.storyContext: Mr. Patel challenges Isha with the final test: design a courtyard using two different regular polygons that tessellate together.

example.problem: Design a tessellation using regular triangles (interior angle 60°) and regular hexagons (interior angle 120°). At each vertex where they meet, angles must sum to 360°. If there are t triangles and h hexagons meeting at a point, find a valid combination of t and h.
example.solution: 60t + 120h = 360. Divide by 60: t + 2h = 6. Solutions: t=6,h=0 (only triangles); t=4,h=1 (4 triangles, 1 hexagon); t=2,h=2 (2 triangles, 2 hexagons); t=0,h=3 (only hexagons). The semi-regular tessellation uses t=2,h=1 or t=4,h=1 combinations.

slides.inSimpleWords: By understanding angles and properties, you can design tessellations that combine different shapes in perfect harmony.

slides.title: Interior vs. Exterior Angles
slides.storyContext: Rohan asks: 'If I walk around a polygon, turning at each corner, how much do I turn in total?' Mr. Patel smiles. 'That's the sum of exterior angles—always 360°!'

example.problem: A regular polygon has interior angles of 144° each. Find: (i) The exterior angle. (ii) The number of sides.
example.solution: (i) Exterior angle = 180° − 144° = 36°. (ii) Number of sides = 360° / 36° = 10. This is a regular decagon.

slides.inSimpleWords: Exterior angles are the 'turns' at each corner. All exterior angles of any polygon sum to exactly 360°.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Polygons are closed shapes with straight sides. A polygon with n sides has sum of angles = (n-2)×180°.
Regular polygons have all sides equal and all angles equal. Each angle = [(n-2)×180°]/n.
Triangles can be classified by sides (equilateral, isosceles, scalene) or by angles (acute, right, obtuse).
Line symmetry: fold and both halves match. Rotational symmetry: rotate and shape matches itself. Point symmetry: 180° rotation looks identical.
Quadrilaterals: square (most symmetric), rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram (least symmetric).
Tessellations are patterns of shapes that fit together perfectly. Only triangles, squares, and hexagons tessellate alone.
Geometry is the language of architecture and design. Symmetry and shapes reveal the hidden order in the world.

slides.inSimpleWords: Geometry is everywhere—in buildings, tiles, and nature. Symmetry and shapes reveal the hidden order. By understanding polygons and their properties, you can design, build, and create anything.

subject: Mathematics
title: Raj's Map Adventure: Where Dots Meet Lines
hook: A young surveyor learns the hidden language of points, lines, and angles in the world around him.

slides.title: Tales by Dots and Lines
slides.storyContext: Raj's grandmother gives him an old map of their village. As he traces the roads with his finger, he discovers that geometry isn't just in textbooks—it's everywhere.

slides.title: The Map That Told a Story
slides.storyContext: One afternoon, Dadi pulls out a yellowed map showing the village paths. 'Every road, every corner tells a story,' she says. Raj notices the map is made of dots marking houses and lines connecting roads. 'That's geometry, beta!' Dadi smiles. Together with Kavi the map-maker, they decide to explore the language of points and lines.

slides.title: What is a Point?
slides.storyContext: Kavi teaches Raj: 'A point is the simplest idea in geometry—a single location with no length, width, or thickness. On a map, each house is marked with a dot, like a point.' Raj marks a dot on paper. 'This represents one exact spot.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: A point has no dimension; it is an exact location in space, marked with a dot.

points.label: Example in life
points.text: The corner of a cricket pitch, the center of a well, the exact spot where you live.

slides.inSimpleWords: A point is a tiny invisible dot that marks one exact place. It has no size—it just shows where something is.

slides.title: What is a Line?
slides.storyContext: Kavi draws two dots on the map and connects them with a straight edge. 'When we connect two points with a ruler, we get a line. But a line extends forever in both directions, even beyond what we draw.' Raj extends the line in his mind, imagining it stretching across the fields.

points.label: Definition
points.text: A line is straight and extends infinitely in both directions. It has length but no width or thickness.

points.label: Notation
points.text: Written as AB (passing through points A and B) or as line ℓ.

points.label: In daily life
points.text: The horizon, a railway track, the edge of a straight road.

slides.inSimpleWords: A line is like a perfectly straight path that goes on and on forever in both directions, even though we can only draw part of it.

slides.title: Line Segments and Rays
slides.storyContext: Raj asks: 'In real life, the road doesn't go on forever. What do we call that?' Kavi nods. 'That's a line segment—a part of a line with two endpoints. And if the road starts from the village center and goes on in one direction? That's a ray!'

points.label: Line Segment
points.text: A part of a line between two endpoints. Has fixed length. Denoted AB or segment AB.

points.label: Ray
points.text: Starts at one point and extends infinitely in one direction. Denoted AB (starting at A, passing through B).

points.label: Compare
points.text: Line (infinite both ways) vs. Segment (finite, two ends) vs. Ray (starts at one point, infinite in one direction).

example.problem: The path from Raj's house to the well is 200 meters. What is this in geometric terms?
example.solution: This is a line segment—it has two endpoints (house and well) and a fixed length (200 m).

slides.inSimpleWords: A line segment is like a rope between two points—you can measure it. A ray is like a torch beam—it starts from one spot and keeps going.

slides.title: Intersecting Lines
slides.storyContext: On the map, two roads cross at the village square. Kavi explains: 'When two lines meet at a point, they intersect. That point is called the point of intersection.' Raj sees this everywhere now—at crossroads, where walls meet, where branches split.

points.label: Definition
points.text: When two lines meet at exactly one point, they are called intersecting lines.

points.label: Point of intersection
points.text: The exact point where two lines cross.

points.label: Real example
points.text: Two roads crossing at a junction form intersecting lines.

slides.inSimpleWords: When two straight paths cross each other at one point, that's called intersecting. The spot where they meet is the intersection point.

slides.title: Parallel Lines
slides.storyContext: Raj traces two railway tracks on the map. 'These never meet, no matter how far they go,' he observes. Kavi smiles, 'Exactly! These are parallel lines—they go in the same direction and never intersect, no matter how far they extend.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: Lines that lie in the same plane and never intersect are called parallel lines.

points.label: Notation
points.text: Line AB is parallel to line CD is written as AB || CD.

points.label: Same distance apart
points.text: Parallel lines maintain the same perpendicular distance at every point.

points.label: Everywhere
points.text: Railway tracks, edges of a door frame, opposite sides of a notebook.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallel lines are like two rails of a railway track—they run side by side forever without ever touching or crossing.

slides.title: Angles: Where Lines Meet
slides.storyContext: Kavi draws two rays starting from the same point on the map. 'The opening between these two rays is called an angle,' she says. 'See how the market road and the temple road form a sharp corner? That's an angle formed by two rays with a common starting point.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: An angle is formed by two rays (or line segments) sharing a common endpoint called the vertex.

points.label: Parts
points.text: Vertex (common point), Arms (the two rays), Angle (the opening between them).

points.label: Notation
points.text: ∠ABC where B is the vertex.

points.label: Measurement
points.text: Angles are measured in degrees (°) using a protractor.

example.problem: Two roads meet at the village square forming a 90° angle. What type of angle is this?
example.solution: This is a right angle (90°). It looks like a square corner, like the corner of a building.

slides.inSimpleWords: An angle is the amount of opening between two lines or rays that start from the same point. Think of it like the pages of an open book—the wider you open it, the bigger the angle.

slides.title: Raj's Angle Discovery
slides.storyContext: Raj uses a protractor to measure the angles between three different roads meeting at the village center. 'These are all different!' he exclaims. Kavi nods. 'Yes, and each angle type has a special name and special properties. Let me teach you.'

slides.title: Types of Angles

points.label: Acute angle
points.text: Measures less than 90°. Examples: 30°, 45°, 60°. Sharp, pointy angle.

points.label: Right angle
points.text: Measures exactly 90°. The corner of a square or rectangle. Often marked with a small square.

points.label: Obtuse angle
points.text: Measures more than 90° but less than 180°. Examples: 120°, 150°. Wide, open angle.

points.label: Straight angle
points.text: Measures exactly 180°. Forms a straight line. No bend at all.

points.label: Reflex angle
points.text: Measures more than 180° but less than 360°. The 'outside' of an obtuse angle.

example.problem: Three angles meet at a point: 60°, 120°, and 80°. What is the fourth angle that completes the full rotation?
example.solution: Around a point, all angles sum to 360°. Fourth angle = 360° - 60° - 120° - 80° = 100°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles have different sizes: acute (sharp), right (square corner), obtuse (wide), straight (flat line), and reflex (more than flat).

slides.title: Complementary and Supplementary Angles

points.label: Complementary angles
points.text: Two angles whose measures add up to 90°. Example: 30° + 60° = 90°.

points.label: Supplementary angles
points.text: Two angles whose measures add up to 180°. Example: 60° + 120° = 180°.

points.label: Vertical angles
points.text: When two lines intersect, opposite angles are equal. These are vertical angles.

example.problem: Two angles are complementary. One angle is 35°. What is the other?
example.solution: If two angles are complementary, they sum to 90°. Other angle = 90° - 35° = 55°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Complementary angles go together to make a right angle (90°). Supplementary angles go together to make a straight line (180°).

slides.title: Perpendicular Lines
slides.storyContext: Kavi draws two roads that meet at a perfect square corner. 'When two lines meet at exactly 90°, they are perpendicular,' she explains. 'They form a right angle—the most common and useful angle in building and design.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: Two lines are perpendicular if they meet at a 90° angle (a right angle).

points.label: Notation
points.text: Line AB is perpendicular to line CD is written as AB ⊥ CD.

points.label: Everywhere
points.text: The corner of a door, edges of a wall and floor, the crosshairs on a map.

example.problem: A vertical wall meets a horizontal floor. What is the angle between them?
example.solution: They are perpendicular, so the angle is 90° (a right angle).

slides.inSimpleWords: Perpendicular lines are like a perfect square corner—they make a 90° angle. This is the most important right angle in geometry.

slides.title: Measuring Angles in the Village
slides.storyContext: Raj uses a protractor to measure angles formed by different roads in his village.

example.problem: Three roads meet at a junction: Road A to the East, Road B at 60° from Road A (counterclockwise), and Road C at 150° from Road A. Find: (i) The angle between Road B and Road C. (ii) Name the type of each angle formed.
example.solution:
(i) Angle between Road B and Road C = 150° - 60° = 90°. This is a right angle.
(ii) Angle ∠(Road A, Road B) = 60° (acute angle, less than 90°). Angle ∠(Road A, Road C) = 150° (obtuse angle, more than 90°).

slides.inSimpleWords: By measuring the angles between roads, we can understand how they turn and intersect at junctions.

slides.title: The Transversal Discovery
slides.storyContext: Raj notices something interesting: when one road (a transversal) crosses two railway tracks (parallel lines), it creates a pattern of angles. 'Kavi, look! The angles match up in a pattern!' Kavi grins. 'Exactly! This is one of geometry's beautiful secrets.'

slides.title: Transversals and Parallel Lines

points.label: Transversal
points.text: A line that intersects two or more lines at different points.

points.label: Corresponding angles
points.text: When a transversal crosses two parallel lines, angles in the same position at each intersection are equal.

points.label: Alternate angles
points.text: Angles on opposite sides of the transversal are equal.

points.label: Co-interior (same-side interior) angles
points.text: Angles on the same side of the transversal and between the parallel lines sum to 180°.

example.problem: A transversal crosses two parallel lines. If one angle is 75°, find: (i) The corresponding angle at the other intersection. (ii) The alternate angle. (iii) The co-interior angle.
example.solution: (i) Corresponding angle = 75° (equal to given angle). (ii) Alternate angle = 75°. (iii) Co-interior angle = 180° - 75° = 105°.

slides.inSimpleWords: When one line crosses two parallel lines, it creates special angle relationships: matching angles are equal, opposite angles are equal, and angles on the same side add to 180°.

slides.title: Angle Bisectors and Perpendicular Bisectors
slides.storyContext: Raj wants to split an angle exactly in half. Kavi shows him: 'Draw a line from the vertex that divides the angle into two equal parts. That's an angle bisector. A perpendicular bisector does the same for a line segment.'

points.label: Angle bisector
points.text: A ray from the vertex of an angle that divides it into two equal angles.

points.label: Perpendicular bisector
points.text: A line that passes through the midpoint of a line segment and is perpendicular to it.

points.label: Construction
points.text: Use a compass and ruler to construct these lines precisely.

example.problem: An angle measures 120°. An angle bisector divides it into two angles. What is the measure of each angle?
example.solution: Each angle = 120° / 2 = 60°.

slides.inSimpleWords: An angle bisector splits an angle exactly in half. A perpendicular bisector is like splitting a line exactly in half and turning perpendicular.

slides.title: Raj's Geometry Challenge
slides.storyContext: Kavi gives Raj a map of the village with several roads. She asks him to identify the geometric figures and relationships.

example.problem:
On Raj's map:
- The path from home to the well is 250 m straight.
- The path from the well to the school is perpendicular (90°) to the first path and is 150 m long.
- The road from school to the market is parallel to the home-to-well path.
(a) What geometric figure do the three paths form?
(b) If the school-to-market road is 250 m, what shape is complete?
(c) Identify all the line segments, rays, and angles in this figure.
example.solution:
(a) The first two paths form a right angle at the well; this is part of a rectangle.
(b) If the school-to-market road is also 250 m and parallel to the first path, the four points (home, well, school, market) form a rectangle.
(c) Line segments: home-to-well, well-to-school, school-to-market, market-to-home. Rays: none shown as complete rays. Angles: 90° at well and school (right angles), 90° at home and market (right angles).

slides.inSimpleWords: Using points, lines, and angles, Raj discovers that the village paths form a perfect rectangle!

slides.title: Building the Village Square
slides.storyContext: Raj helps Kavi design the new village square. Using his knowledge of points, lines, and angles, they plan where to place roads, benches, and monuments.

example.problem: The village square is built at the intersection of Main Road (running North-South) and Market Road (running East-West). Two diagonal paths also cross the square. Find: (i) How many angles are formed at the center where all four roads meet? (ii) If the two diagonal paths bisect the right angles, what is the measure of each resulting angle?
example.solution: (i) Four roads create 8 angles at the center (each pair of adjacent roads forms one angle, and opposite angles are equal). Actually, any number of lines meeting at a point create 2n angles where n is the number of lines. (ii) Right angles = 90°. Bisecting a 90° angle gives two 45° angles.

slides.inSimpleWords: By carefully placing points, lines, and angles, Raj and Kavi design a beautiful village square that's both functional and geometric.

slides.title: Measuring Distance: From Theory to Practice
slides.storyContext: Raj needs to find the shortest distance from his house to the well. Kavi shows him: 'The shortest path between two points is always a straight line—that's a line segment. Let's measure it!'

slides.title: Distance and Midpoint

points.label: Distance
points.text: The length of a line segment connecting two points. Measured in units (cm, m, km, etc.).

points.label: Midpoint
points.text: The point exactly halfway along a line segment. It divides the segment into two equal parts.

points.label: Pythagorean theorem preview
points.text: For a right triangle with legs a and b and hypotenuse c: a² + b² = c². Used to find distances.

example.problem: A line segment goes from point A (at 0 meters) to point B (at 50 meters). Where is the midpoint?
example.solution: Midpoint = (0 + 50) / 2 = 25 meters. The midpoint is at 25 meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: The distance between two points is measured along a straight line. The midpoint is the exact middle of that line.

slides.title: Adjacent and Vertically Opposite Angles
slides.storyContext: At the crossroads, Raj observes four angles formed by two intersecting roads. 'The angles next to each other are adjacent. The ones across from each other are special too!'

points.label: Adjacent angles
points.text: Angles that share a common vertex and a common arm (side), but no common interior points.

points.label: Vertically opposite angles
points.text: When two lines intersect, the angles across from each other are equal. These are vertical angles.

points.label: Linear pair
points.text: Two adjacent angles on a straight line that sum to 180°.

example.problem: Two lines intersect. One angle measures 75°. Find all four angles.
example.solution: Two angles are 75° (opposite to each other). The other two are 180° − 75° = 105° each (also opposite to each other).

slides.inSimpleWords: When lines cross, opposite angles are always equal. Next-door angles always add up to 180°.

slides.title: Angle Sum in Geometric Figures
slides.storyContext: Raj draws different shapes and discovers a pattern: no matter the shape, angles have predictable sums.

points.label: Triangle angles
points.text: The sum of angles in any triangle = 180°.

points.label: Quadrilateral angles
points.text: The sum of angles in any quadrilateral = 360°.

points.label: General polygon
points.text: Sum of angles = (n − 2) × 180° for an n-sided polygon.

example.problem: A triangle has angles 60° and 70°. Find the third angle.
example.solution: Sum of angles in a triangle = 180°. Third angle = 180° − 60° − 70° = 50°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every triangle's angles add to 180°. Every quadrilateral's angles add to 360°. This pattern continues for all polygons.

slides.title: Constructing Geometric Figures
slides.storyContext: Kavi teaches Raj to construct perfect geometric figures using only a compass and straightedge. 'You can draw perfect perpendiculars, bisect angles, and even create regular polygons!'

slides.title: Basic Geometric Constructions

points.label: Perpendicular bisector
points.text: A line perpendicular to a segment passing through its midpoint. Constructed using compass and straightedge.

points.label: Angle bisector construction
points.text: To bisect an angle: use compass centered at vertex to mark equal arcs; connect vertex to the point where arcs intersect.

points.label: Copying an angle
points.text: Can create an identical angle at a different location using compass and straightedge.

example.problem: How do you construct a 45° angle if you have a 90° right angle?
example.solution: Bisect the 90° angle. The angle bisector divides it into two 45° angles.

slides.inSimpleWords: With a compass and straightedge, you can create perfect copies of angles, bisect them, and construct perpendiculars precisely.

slides.title: Complex Map Reading with Multiple Lines
slides.storyContext: Raj's village expands. Now there are multiple intersecting and parallel roads. He uses angle relationships to map the entire network.

example.problem: Three roads intersect at a central point: Main Road, Market Road, and Temple Road. Main and Market Roads form a 75° angle. Market and Temple Roads form a 110° angle. What angle do Main and Temple Roads form?
example.solution: Going counterclockwise: Main to Market = 75°, Market to Temple = 110°, so Main to Temple = 75° + 110° = 185°. But angles around a point sum to 360°, so the 'other' angle (going the other way) = 360° − 185° = 175°. Both angles are valid depending on which direction you measure.

slides.inSimpleWords: When three or more lines meet at a point, all angles around that point must sum to 360°.

slides.title: What Raj Learned
slides.storyContext: As the sun sets, Raj folds his map and thanks Kavi. Dadi smiles: 'Now you speak the language of geometry. You see the world in points, lines, and angles.'

points.text: A point marks an exact location with no size.
A line extends infinitely in both directions; a line segment has two endpoints; a ray starts at one point and goes infinitely in one direction.
When two lines meet at one point, they intersect at that point.
Parallel lines never meet and always stay the same distance apart. Perpendicular lines meet at 90°.
An angle is formed by two rays sharing a common endpoint (vertex) and is measured in degrees.
Angle types: acute (< 90°), right (= 90°), obtuse (> 90° but < 180°), straight (= 180°).
A transversal crossing parallel lines creates equal corresponding angles and alternate angles, with co-interior angles summing to 180°.
Adjacent angles share a vertex and side; vertically opposite angles (formed by intersecting lines) are equal.
Triangles have angles summing to 180°; quadrilaterals sum to 360°; general n-gons sum to (n−2)×180°.
Geometry is not just theory—it's in roads, buildings, fields, and the world around us.

slides.inSimpleWords: Points, lines, angles, and their relationships help us understand and describe the shapes we see every day. The world is built on geometry.

subject: Mathematics
title: Meera's Market Mystery: The Algebra of Trade
hook: A young vendor learns to use algebra to solve real trading puzzles in the bustling village market.

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: Meera's friend who helps keep track of goods

slides.title: Algebra Play: A Merchant's Secret
slides.storyContext: At the village market, Meera watches vendors trade goods and money. Her father shows her a ledger filled with numbers and letters. 'This is algebra,' he says. 'It's how we solve trading problems when we don't know all the answers yet.'

image.alt: Algebra Play: A Merchant's Secret — Algebra Play

slides.title: The Mystery of the Missing Mangoes
slides.storyContext: One morning, Meera finds a note on the fruit stand: 'I brought some mangoes. I sold half of them and 5 extra. Now I have 10 mangoes left. How many did I start with?' Uncle Ravi laughs. 'That's an algebra puzzle! We use a letter, like x, to stand for the unknown number. Then we solve to find the answer.'

image.alt: The Mystery of the Missing Mangoes — Algebra Play

slides.title: What is a Variable?
slides.storyContext: Uncle Ravi explains: 'In the market, sometimes we know the price but not the quantity. Sometimes we know the quantity but not the total cost. We use a letter—x, y, or any letter—to represent the unknown number we're trying to find.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: A variable is a letter (like x, y, a, b) that represents an unknown number in a mathematical statement.

points.label: Purpose
points.text: Variables help us write general rules and solve problems where one value is unknown.

points.label: Real example
points.text: If I have some apples and buy 5 more, I now have x + 5 apples, where x is the original count.

slides.inSimpleWords: A variable is like a mystery box with an unknown number inside. We use a letter to represent it until we figure out what's inside.

image.alt: What is a Variable? — Algebra Play

slides.title: Algebraic Expressions
slides.storyContext: Meera starts writing the trading information as mathematical sentences. 'If a mango costs ₹y and I buy 3 mangoes, I spend 3y rupees,' she says. Priya nods. 'That's an algebraic expression—a mix of numbers, variables, and operations!'

points.label: Definition
points.text: An algebraic expression is a combination of numbers, variables, and mathematical operations (+, −, ×, ÷).

points.label: Terms
points.text: Each part separated by + or − is called a term. In 3x + 5, '3x' and '5' are the terms.

points.label: Coefficient
points.text: The number multiplied by the variable. In 3x, the coefficient is 3.

example.problem: Write an expression: A vendor has x bunches of carrots. He sells 8 bunches. How many does he have left?
example.solution: He has x − 8 bunches left. This is an algebraic expression where x is the original number and we subtract 8.

slides.inSimpleWords: An algebraic expression is like a sentence in the language of math, using letters and numbers mixed together with operations.

slides.title: Simplifying Makes It Clear
slides.storyContext: Meera notices that when she combines similar items in her inventory, the count becomes clearer. 'I have 3 bunches of bananas and then buy 5 more bunches. That's 3b + 5b = 8b bunches total!' Uncle Ravi smiles. 'Yes! You're simplifying by combining like terms.'

slides.title: Like Terms and Simplifying Expressions

points.label: Like terms
points.text: Terms that have the same variable raised to the same power. Example: 3x and 5x are like terms; 3x and 3y are not.

points.label: Combining like terms
points.text: Add or subtract the coefficients; keep the variable. 3x + 5x = 8x.

points.label: Constants
points.text: Numbers with no variables are also like terms. 7 + 3 = 10.

example.problem: Simplify: 4x + 7 − 2x + 3
example.solution: Combine like terms: (4x − 2x) + (7 + 3) = 2x + 10.

slides.inSimpleWords: Like terms are twins—they have the same variable. We can add or subtract them to make the expression simpler.

slides.title: Order of Operations with Variables (BODMAS/PEMDAS)
slides.storyContext: Meera calculates the cost of buying fruit. 'I buy 3 bunches of carrots at ₹x each, plus 2 bunches of tomatoes at ₹y each, plus ₹10 delivery charge. That's 3x + 2y + 10. But in what order do I evaluate this?'

points.label: BODMAS rule
points.text: Brackets, Orders (powers), Division and Multiplication (left to right), Addition and Subtraction (left to right).

points.label: Example
points.text: In 3 + 2 × x, multiply first: 3 + (2x). Don't add first.

points.label: With brackets
points.text: In 2(x + 5), the brackets are first: 2x + 10.

example.problem: Evaluate: 5 + 3 × 2 − 4
example.solution: Multiply first: 5 + 6 − 4 = 7. (Not 5 + 3 = 8, then 8 × 2 = 16, then 16 − 4 = 12.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Follow BODMAS to know which operation to do first. Brackets first, then powers, then multiply/divide, then add/subtract.

slides.title: Linear Equations
slides.storyContext: Uncle Ravi writes on his slate: 'When an expression equals something, we have an equation. For example, if Meera had x apples and now has 15 after selling some, we might write: x − 5 = 15. This is an equation.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: An equation is a mathematical statement saying two expressions are equal, shown with an '=' sign.

points.label: Linear equation
points.text: An equation with variables raised to the power of 1 only (no x², x³, etc.). Form: ax + b = c

points.label: Example
points.text: 2x + 3 = 11 is a linear equation. The variable x appears to the first power.

points.label: Parts
points.text: Left side (2x + 3), equals sign (=), right side (11).

slides.inSimpleWords: An equation is like a balance scale. The left side equals the right side. Our job is to find the value of the variable that makes this balance true.

slides.title: Solving Linear Equations
slides.storyContext: Meera asks, 'Now how do I find x?' Uncle Ravi explains: 'We use the golden rule: whatever we do to one side of the equation, we must do to the other side. Keep doing this until x stands alone on one side.'

points.label: Goal
points.text: Isolate the variable (get it alone on one side of the equation).

points.label: Operations
points.text: Use opposite operations: to undo addition, subtract; to undo subtraction, add; to undo multiplication, divide; to undo division, multiply.

points.label: The rule
points.text: What you do to the left side, you must do to the right side—to keep the balance.

points.label: Steps
points.text: 1. Simplify both sides. 2. Move variable terms to one side. 3. Move constants to the other. 4. Solve for the variable.

example.problem: Solve: 2x + 5 = 13
example.solution:
Step 1: 2x + 5 = 13
Step 2: Subtract 5 from both sides: 2x = 13 − 5 = 8
Step 3: Divide both sides by 2: x = 8 ÷ 2 = 4
Answer: x = 4. Check: 2(4) + 5 = 8 + 5 = 13 ✓

slides.inSimpleWords: To solve an equation, we do the same operation to both sides until the variable is alone. It's like keeping a scale balanced while moving weights around.

slides.title: Multi-Step Equations at the Market
slides.storyContext: Meera faces her first real puzzle: 'I spent ₹280 buying apples and bananas. Apples cost ₹30 per kg, bananas ₹40 per kg. If I bought 2 kg of apples, how many kg of bananas did I buy?' Uncle Ravi hands her a notepad. 'Write the equation and solve it step by step.'

slides.title: Real-World Problem Solving
slides.storyContext: Meera faces a real puzzle at the market. 'I spent ₹120 buying some apples at ₹x per apple and 10 guavas at ₹8 each. Total was ₹120, so 3x + 80 = 120. Find the price of one apple.' Uncle Ravi smiles. 'Perfect! Solve it.'

points.label: Step 1: Read carefully
points.text: Identify what you know and what you need to find.

points.label: Step 2: Write the equation
points.text: Translate the words into an algebraic equation.

points.label: Step 3: Solve
points.text: Use algebraic steps to isolate the variable.

points.label: Step 4: Check
points.text: Substitute your answer back to verify it's correct.

example.problem: Meera's mother gives her ₹500. She spends ₹100 on a notebook and the rest on pens at ₹25 each. How many pens can she buy?
example.solution:
Let x = number of pens.
Money for pens = 500 − 100 = 400
Equation: 25x = 400
Solve: x = 400 ÷ 25 = 16
Answer: She can buy 16 pens.

slides.inSimpleWords: To solve word problems, change the story into an equation, then solve it step by step.

slides.title: Equations with Variables on Both Sides
slides.storyContext: Priya asks Meera: 'What if I buy apples at ₹x each, and you buy apples at ₹y each, but we end up spending the same amount? Then 3x = 5y. How do we solve that?'

points.label: Goal
points.text: Move all variables to one side and constants to the other.

points.label: Steps
points.text: 1. Collect variable terms on the left (or right). 2. Collect constants on the other side. 3. Simplify and solve.

points.label: Example form
points.text: 3x + 5 = x + 15 becomes 3x − x = 15 − 5, then 2x = 10, so x = 5.

example.problem: Solve: 4x + 8 = 2x + 20
example.solution:
Subtract 2x from both sides: 4x − 2x + 8 = 20
2x + 8 = 20
Subtract 8: 2x = 12
Divide by 2: x = 6
Check: 4(6) + 8 = 32 and 2(6) + 20 = 32 ✓

slides.inSimpleWords: When the variable appears on both sides, move one copy to the other side using subtraction first, then solve.

slides.title: The Great Market Exchange
slides.storyContext: At the market fair, Meera solves trading puzzles to win prizes.

example.problem: At the market, a bundle of 5 pens and 3 notebooks costs ₹185. A bundle of 2 pens and 1 notebook costs ₹70. Using separate equations: (i) Let p = cost of one pen and n = cost of one notebook. Write two equations. (ii) If the cost of one notebook is ₹45, find the cost of one pen.
example.solution:
(i) Equation 1: 5p + 3n = 185 (from the first bundle)
    Equation 2: 2p + n = 70 (from the second bundle)
(ii) Substitute n = 45 into Equation 2:
    2p + 45 = 70
    2p = 70 − 45 = 25
    p = 12.5
    Answer: One pen costs ₹12.50, one notebook costs ₹45.

slides.inSimpleWords: By writing multiple equations, we can solve mysteries with more than one unknown.

image.alt: The Great Market Exchange — Algebra Play

slides.title: Systems of Equations in Trading
slides.storyContext: Meera faces a complex trading puzzle involving two unknowns. She writes down two separate equations and realizes she can solve them together by substitution or elimination. Uncle Ravi watches proudly as she works through the system.

slides.title: Systems of Linear Equations (Introduction)

points.label: Definition
points.text: A system of linear equations is a set of two or more equations with the same variables. We solve to find values that satisfy all equations simultaneously.

points.label: Two main methods
points.text: Substitution (solve one equation for a variable, substitute into the other) and Elimination (add or subtract equations to eliminate a variable).

points.label: Graphical understanding
points.text: Each equation is a line on a graph. The solution is where the lines intersect (one solution), or they never intersect (no solution), or they're the same line (infinite solutions).

example.problem: Solve the system: x + y = 10 and x − y = 4
example.solution:
Add the two equations: (x + y) + (x − y) = 10 + 4
2x = 14
x = 7
Substitute into first equation: 7 + y = 10, so y = 3
Answer: x = 7, y = 3.

slides.inSimpleWords: A system of equations has two or more equations with the same variables. We solve them together to find values that work for all equations.

slides.title: Substitution Method in Detail
slides.storyContext: Meera learns the substitution method: 'If I know that x = 2y from one equation, I can replace x with 2y everywhere in the other equation. Then I have just one variable to solve!'

points.label: Step 1
points.text: Solve one equation for one variable (e.g., x = 3y + 5).

points.label: Step 2
points.text: Substitute that expression into the other equation.

points.label: Step 3
points.text: Solve the resulting single-variable equation.

points.label: Step 4
points.text: Substitute back to find the other variable.

example.problem: Solve: x + 2y = 7 and x = y + 1
example.solution:
From the second equation, x = y + 1.
Substitute into the first: (y + 1) + 2y = 7
3y + 1 = 7
3y = 6
y = 2
Substitute back: x = 2 + 1 = 3
Answer: x = 3, y = 2.

slides.inSimpleWords: The substitution method: solve one equation for a variable, then plug that into the other equation. It's like solving a puzzle by replacing unknowns with known relationships.

slides.title: Meera's Final Challenge
slides.storyContext: Uncle Ravi gives Meera the hardest puzzle yet. 'Solve this, and you're a true merchant!',

example.problem: Meera buys apples at ₹x per kg and bananas at ₹y per kg. She buys 3 kg of apples and 5 kg of bananas for ₹415. Later, she buys 2 kg of apples and 3 kg of bananas for ₹250. Find the cost of apples and bananas per kg.
example.solution:
Equation 1: 3x + 5y = 415
Equation 2: 2x + 3y = 250

From Equation 2: 2x = 250 − 3y, so x = (250 − 3y)/2

Substitute into Equation 1:
3[(250 − 3y)/2] + 5y = 415
(750 − 9y)/2 + 5y = 415
Multiply by 2: 750 − 9y + 10y = 830
750 + y = 830
y = 80

Substitute y = 80 into Equation 2:
2x + 3(80) = 250
2x + 240 = 250
2x = 10
x = 5

Answer: Apples cost ₹5 per kg, bananas cost ₹80 per kg.

slides.inSimpleWords: By solving two equations together, Meera discovers the exact price of each fruit!

slides.title: Mastering Algebra in the Market
slides.storyContext: Meera uses algebra every day now: calculating costs, finding discounts, solving trading puzzles, and managing inventory. Her ledger is filled with equations and solutions.

example.problem: The market hosts a sale. Shirts cost ₹a each, pants cost ₹b each. On Monday, 4 shirts and 2 pants sold for ₹1000 total. On Tuesday, 3 shirts and 5 pants sold for ₹1400 total. Find the cost of one shirt and one pair of pants.
example.solution:
Equation 1: 4a + 2b = 1000
Equation 2: 3a + 5b = 1400

From Equation 1, divide by 2: 2a + b = 500, so b = 500 − 2a

Substitute into Equation 2:
3a + 5(500 − 2a) = 1400
3a + 2500 − 10a = 1400
−7a = −1100
a = 1100/7 ≈ 157.14

Substitute back: b = 500 − 2(157.14) = 500 − 314.28 = 185.72

Answer: Shirt costs ₹157.14, pants cost ₹185.72 (or rounding to market prices).

slides.inSimpleWords: Algebra helps solve any trading puzzle: multiple prices, multiple quantities, multiple equations—all solvable with patience and the right steps.

slides.title: Inequalities at the Market
slides.storyContext: Meera realizes not all market situations have exact answers. 'I need to buy at least 10 kg of vegetables but spend less than ₹500. How can I write this mathematically?' Uncle Ravi smiles. 'That's an inequality—it uses symbols like < and >.'

slides.title: Inequalities and Their Properties

points.label: Inequality symbols
points.text: < (less than), > (greater than), ≤ (less than or equal), ≥ (greater than or equal), ≠ (not equal).

points.label: Solving inequalities
points.text: Similar to equations, but if you multiply or divide by a negative number, flip the inequality sign.

points.label: Solution set
points.text: An inequality has multiple solutions. Example: x > 5 means x could be 5.1, 6, 10, 100, etc.

example.problem: Solve: 3x − 5 > 10
example.solution:
Add 5 to both sides: 3x > 15
Divide by 3: x > 5
Solution: Any value greater than 5.

slides.inSimpleWords: Inequalities show when one value is bigger or smaller than another. Solving them is like solving equations, but the answer is a range, not a single number.

slides.title: Factoring Algebraic Expressions
slides.storyContext: Priya notices a pattern: '3x + 3y = 3(x + y). We're pulling out the common factor 3!' Meera realizes this makes expressions simpler.

points.label: Common factor
points.text: A number or variable that divides evenly into every term.

points.label: Factoring
points.text: Writing an expression as a product of its factors. Example: 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3).

points.label: Checking
points.text: Expand the factored form to verify it equals the original.

example.problem: Factor: 12a² + 8a
example.solution:
Find the greatest common factor of 12a² and 8a: it's 4a.
12a² + 8a = 4a(3a + 2)
Check: 4a(3a + 2) = 12a² + 8a ✓

slides.inSimpleWords: Factoring is like reversing multiplication. Instead of expanding, you compress an expression by pulling out common numbers or variables.

slides.title: Expanding Brackets and Distributive Property
slides.storyContext: Uncle Ravi teaches: 'If Meera buys 3 bundles, each containing x apples and y oranges, she gets 3x apples and 3y oranges. That's the distributive property: 3(x + y) = 3x + 3y.'

points.label: Distributive property
points.text: a(b + c) = ab + ac. Multiply the outside term by each term inside.

points.label: FOIL (for binomials)
points.text: (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd. (First, Outer, Inner, Last)

points.label: Common mistakes
points.text: Don't forget to distribute to every term. a(b + c + d) = ab + ac + ad.

example.problem: Expand: 2(3x + 5) and (x + 2)(x + 3)

slides.inSimpleWords: Expanding means multiplying brackets. The distributive property lets you multiply one number by every term inside the brackets.

slides.title: Elimination Method for Systems
slides.storyContext: Meera learns a new way to solve systems: add or subtract equations to eliminate one variable entirely.

example.problem:
Solve using elimination:
2x + 3y = 12
x + 2y = 7
example.solution:
Multiply the second equation by 2 to match x coefficients:
2x + 3y = 12
2x + 4y = 14

Subtract the first from the second:
(2x + 4y) − (2x + 3y) = 14 − 12
y = 2

Substitute back: x + 2(2) = 7, so x = 3
Answer: x = 3, y = 2

slides.inSimpleWords: The elimination method: multiply equations so one variable has matching coefficients, then add or subtract to eliminate it and solve.

slides.title: Graphing Linear Equations
slides.storyContext: Meera draws a line on graph paper: 'If I plot y = 2x + 1, it's a straight line! And where it crosses the y-axis is 1. The slope is 2, meaning it rises 2 units for every 1 unit across.'

points.label: Slope-intercept form
points.text: y = mx + b, where m is the slope and b is the y-intercept (where the line crosses the y-axis).

points.label: Slope
points.text: The steepness of the line. Slope = (change in y) / (change in x) = rise/run.

points.label: y-intercept
points.text: The point where the line crosses the y-axis (set x = 0).

example.problem: Find the slope and y-intercept of: y = −3x + 5
example.solution: Slope (m) = −3. Y-intercept (b) = 5, so the point is (0, 5).

slides.inSimpleWords: Linear equations graph as straight lines. The slope tells you how steep the line is; the y-intercept tells you where it crosses the y-axis.

slides.title: The Power of Algebra in Predictions
slides.storyContext: Meera uses her algebra skills to predict next month's profits. 'If I model daily sales as y = 50x + 100, where x is the number of days, I can predict sales for any day!' Her father is impressed.

slides.title: Meera's Algebra Mastery
slides.storyContext: As the sun sets at the market, Meera writes in her new ledger book, knowing she can now solve any trading puzzle.

points.text: A variable (like x or y) is a letter representing an unknown number.
An algebraic expression combines numbers, variables, and operations (e.g., 3x + 5).
Like terms have the same variable and power. Combine them by adding/subtracting coefficients.
Follow BODMAS: Brackets, Orders, Division, Multiplication, Addition, Subtraction.
A linear equation sets two expressions equal (e.g., 3x + 5 = 20). Solve by isolating the variable.
Inequalities use <, >, ≤, ≥, ≠ and show ranges of solutions. Flip the inequality sign when multiplying/dividing by negatives.
Factoring extracts common factors. Expanding distributes multiplication across brackets.
A system of equations has multiple equations with multiple variables. Solve using substitution or elimination.
Linear equations graph as straight lines with slope m and y-intercept b in the form y = mx + b.
Check your answer by substituting it back into the original equation(s).
Real-world problems translate into equations and inequalities. Algebra is the language of the market and the world.

slides.inSimpleWords: Algebra is a powerful tool that turns mysteries and unknowns into solvable puzzles. With variables, expressions, equations, inequalities, and graphing, we can answer almost any question about trade, prices, and quantities. From simple equations to complex systems and predictions, algebra is the key to understanding and solving real-world problems.
